bib.title: Does Prompt Formatting Have Any Impact on LLM Performance?

question: How much does the global format of a prompt (plain text, Markdown, YAML, JSON) change the performance, consistency and cross-model transferability of OpenAI GPT models?
hypothesis: Implied: prompt format is not performance-neutral, and larger models (GPT-4) are less sensitive than GPT-3.5.
contributions: First comparison of the impact of different prompt formats on GPT models across various tasks, examining plain text, Markdown, YAML, and JSON.
An extensive analysis of prompt formatting effects on GPT models across multiple-choice questions, code generation, and translation.
An evaluation of GPT model iterations via Azure OpenAI, showing GPT-4-turbo is less susceptible to prompt structure variations than earlier models.

method.summary: The same prompt content (persona, task instructions, examples, output format instructions, user ask) was rendered in four formats (plain text, Markdown, YAML, JSON) and run on four Azure OpenAI GPT models across six benchmarks. Sensitivity is tested with one-sided matched-pair t-tests between best and worst format, consistency with identical-answer rate between format pairs, and transferability with IoU of top-format sets.
method.task: Prompt-format sensitivity evaluation: multiple-choice QA, NER, code generation, function reverse-engineering, code translation

datasets.name: MMLU
datasets.split: test set for evaluation; dev set (5 questions per subject) as few-shot examples

datasets.name: FIND (strings category)
datasets.split: strings category; 5 input/output pairs per function randomly sampled from the provided test strings

datasets.name: CODEXGLUE (Java to C#, C# to Java)
HumanEval-X (Java to Python)
datasets.size: 164 data samples used (dataset has 820 in total)
datasets.preprocessing: declaration and canonical-solution combined to form the full function in each language

inference.temperature: 0 for MMLU (stated); other tasks not stated (FIND follows Schwettmann et al. settings)
inference.samples: not stated; one run per model-format-benchmark apparently, with significance via matched-pair t-test over test items
inference.prompting: Five components (persona, task instructions, examples, output format instructions, user ask), identical content across formats; MMLU uses 5 dev-set few-shot examples per subject; NER prompt asks for chain of thought first, then final answer

parameters.iou_top_template_rule: templates statistically indistinguishable from best by matched-pair t-test

metrics.name: Task score
metrics.definition: MMLU accuracy; HumanEval pass@1; NER Finance: whether the LLM outputs each entity in order; FIND string indicator metric (share of test cases passed); CODEXGLUE and HumanEval-X BLEU

metrics.name: Sensitivity
metrics.definition: Max and Min of s(p_i,T) over templates, with one-sided matched-pair t-test between best and worst format

metrics.name: Consistency
metrics.definition: C(Pa,Pb) = (1/N) sum 1(A_Pa(x_i) = A_Pb(x_i)), proportion of test samples with identical answers under two templates (Shu et al., 2023)

metrics.name: IoU
metrics.definition: |Pm1 ∩ Pm2| / |Pm1 ∪ Pm2| over sets of top-performing (statistically indistinguishable) templates for two models

metrics.name: Coefficient of Mean Deviation (CMD)
metrics.definition: sum |s(p_i) - mean s| / (n * mean s) across templates

baselines: Plain text template as default format; models compared against each other
eval.protocol: Per-model, per-benchmark comparison of four formats; one-sided matched-pair t-test best vs worst; the paper does not report seeds or repeats.

availability.data: Public benchmarks only; prompts for NER Finance shown in Appendix C

prompts.purpose: Plain-text template skeleton (Table 2); Markdown, YAML and JSON skeletons use headers/keys Persona, Instructions, Examples, Output Format, User Question/ask
NER Finance system prompt, plain text version
prompts.text: System: You are a annotator working for large financial data company and are tasked with extracting named entities from financial documents who follows strict guidelines for quality and formatting. The following sentence is from a financial document. List the named entities in the order they appear in the sentence. If an entity appears multiple times, list it multiples times. Entities should be stated in the format NAME - TYPE where TYPE can be PERSON, ORGANIZATION, or LOCATION. State your final answer as a comma-separated list of entities enclosed in square brackets. Example: [Bank - ORGANIZATION, Borrower - PERSON]. If there are no entities found, state your final answer as 'No entities found'. Provide your chain of thought first and then respond with your final answer. Here is an example: {ICL EXAMPLE INPUT} {ICL EXAMPLE SOLUTION} User: {INPUT}
prompts.where: Appendix C (Markdown, YAML and JSON versions follow on the next pages)

evidence.quote: For MMLU, we set the temperature to zero to eliminate response variability.

results.claim: GPT-3.5-turbo accuracy on one MMLU international-law example set rose 42% going from Markdown to JSON.
results.setup: Figure 1, GPT-35-turbo-16k-0613, MMLU international law multiple-choice questions, JSON vs Markdown
results.quote: Accuracy goes up by 42% for JSON compared to Markdown.
results.note: Subset result; the full-MMLU gap is 50.7 to 59.4 (Table 3), about 8.7 points.

results.claim: Abstract states GPT-3.5-turbo performance varies by up to 40% in a code translation task depending on template.
results.quote: GPT-3.5-turbo’s performance varies by up to 40% in a code translation task depending on the prompt template
results.note: Does not match the paper's own tables: CODEXGLUE Java2CS BLEU goes 66.46 (plain) to 78.37 (JSON) in Table 8, about 18% relative or 11.9 points; HumanEval-X goes 62.95 to 69.82 (Table 7), about 11%. The only ~40-50% swings are on HumanEval code generation (40.24 to 59.76, Table 4).

results.claim: GPT-3.5 HumanEval pass@1 differs strongly by format: plain text 40.24 vs JSON 59.76 for gpt-35-turbo-0613.
results.setup: HumanEval, gpt-35-turbo-0613, JSON vs plain text

results.claim: MMLU accuracy for GPT-3.5-turbo is best with JSON (59.7) and worst with Markdown (50.0).
results.table: Table 1, row MMLU, GPT-35-turbo-0613 Max (JSON) 59.7 / Min (Markdown) 50.0

results.claim: GPT-4-1106-preview MMLU is best with Markdown (81.2) and worst with JSON (73.9): a drop of about 7 points.
results.table: Table 1, row MMLU, GPT-4-1106-preview Max (Markdown) 81.2 / Min (JSON) 73.9

results.claim: GPT-4-32k-0613 collapses on HumanEval with JSON (21.95 vs 76.22 plain text); the authors say it writes chain of thought but does not go on to produce the code.
results.setup: HumanEval, gpt-4-32k-0613, JSON vs plain text
results.quote: most of the time the model would generate chain of thought in plain text, but did not continue with actually generating the code.
results.note: Prose in Section 3.2 says the improvement is 'over 300%' when switching JSON to plain text; the table numbers give (76.22-21.95)/21.95 = about 247% (3.47x ratio). Hypothesis offered: laziness in task completion fixed in the 0125 GPT-4-turbo.

results.claim: On FIND, GPT-3.5 models gain about 200% from Markdown to plain text (prose); the table gives 5.19 to 15.9 for gpt-35-turbo-0613.
results.table: Table 6, rows markdown (5.19) and plaintext (15.9), column gpt-35-turbo-0613
results.note: (15.9-5.19)/5.19 = 206%, consistent with the prose 200%. Table 1 lists Max 15.9 and Min 5.2.

results.claim: Format differences are statistically significant for almost every model-benchmark pair; the one exception is GPT-4-1106-preview on HumanEval (p = 0.055).
results.setup: One-sided matched-pair t-test, best vs worst format, HumanEval, GPT-4-1106-preview
results.note: Table 1 caption says all p-values are below 0.05 except GPT-4-1106 HumanEval; the text says p-values are 'mostly below 0.01', yet Table 1 also has 0.001 and '< 0.0269' (FIND, GPT-4-1106) entries.

results.claim: GPT-3.5-turbo models are not consistent across formats on MMLU: scores below 0.5, and only 16% identical responses between Markdown and JSON.
results.note: Text of the quote wraps across lines: 'only 16% identical responses between Markdown and JSON formats.' GPT-4 consistency scores exceed 0.5 (read from Fig 2, not in text per cell).

results.claim: Prompt-format preferences do not transfer across model series: IoU of top templates is often below 0.2 across series and above 0.7 within a sub-series.
results.setup: Top templates per model, NER Finance (Fig 3) plus MMLU and FIND (Fig 7)
results.quote: we found low compatibility between different model series, with IoU often below 0.2.
results.note: Same-sub-series pairs (gpt-35-turbo-16k-0613 vs gpt-35-turbo-0613) show IoU 'over 0.7'.

results.claim: GPT-3.5-turbo preferred JSON and GPT-4 preferred Markdown in the paper's summary of Fig 5; no universally optimal format.
results.quote: GPT-3.5-turbo prefers JSON, whereas GPT-4 favors Markdown.
results.note: Not uniform in the tables: GPT-4-1106 NER best is YAML (53.8), GPT-4 FIND best is plain text (Table 6, gpt-4-32k 21.87), and Table 5 GPT-3.5 NER best is plain text (37.20). The preference is benchmark dependent.

results.claim: Coefficient of mean deviation is lower for GPT-4: GPT-4-1106-preview stays below 0.036 on all benchmarks, GPT-3.5 ranges 0.035 to 0.176.
results.quote: maintaining a perfor- mance dispersion consistently below 0.036 across all benchmarks
results.note: Text also says GPT-4-32k-0613 has 'CMDs not exceeding 0.043' while the same section says its HumanEval CMD is 'extremely high' (JSON 21.95 vs about 76/76/68 for others); computing CMD from Table 4 gives about 0.32, so the 0.043 bound cannot hold for HumanEval. GPT-3.5 lower bound 0.035 is below the GPT-4-1106 upper bound 0.036.

results.claim: Larger models are more robust: the sensitivity is similar across MMLU domains, so it is not tied to a particular skill.
results.setup: MMLU per-domain breakdown (humanities, social science, STEM, other), Fig 5
results.quote: Model performance is consistently influenced by prompt formatting across various tasks, regardless of the specific skills or knowledge required.
results.note: Size claim rests on GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4 only; GPT-4 size is assumed, not published.

limits: Only OpenAI GPT models (four Azure variants); the authors list LLaMA, Gemini, PaLM and Phi as future work.
HTML and XML formats were not tried, though common in training data.
All other prompt elements were held fixed; interaction with few-shot count or instruction precision was not studied.
No repeats, seeds, sampling temperature (except MMLU temperature 0), max tokens or API parameters are reported, so a rerun cannot be matched exactly; models are dated Azure snapshots.
Significance testing is best-vs-worst of four formats chosen after seeing the data (selection effect), with no multiple-comparison correction.
Prose percentages (40% code translation, over 300% HumanEval) do not match the tables; the 'size' explanation is inferred since GPT-4 parameters are unpublished.

Table 1 label mismatches: HumanEval-X GPT-3.5 Max is labelled YAML (69.8) though Table 7 shows Markdown 69.82/69.84 above YAML 69.05; CODEXGLUE Java2CS Max is JSON 78.4 while Table 8 has YAML 78.28 and Markdown 78.10 close behind.

terms.definition: How much the choice of prompt template changes a model's task score, tested by max vs min template with matched-pair t-test
Proportion of test samples that yield identical responses for two prompt templates
Intersection-over-union of the sets of top-performing templates for two models
Mean absolute deviation of template scores divided by the mean score
